children.text: Ten days
is not enough to see "all of Egypt."
As a first trip it is a very good length. Less strained than seven, less of a long break than fourteen.
Cairo
and
Giza
Aswan
Abu Simbel
, the Nile transfer,
Luxor
— not just passing through, with a little breath left.
What matters at this length is not giving in to temptation.
Alexandria
is reachable. The Red Sea fits. The White Desert is not impossible. Add them all and ten days becomes a transfer table. To make a really strong first trip, concentrate on the Nile axis.
Cairo and Giza. Aswan. Abu Simbel. Luxor.
Enough. Treated carefully, ten days will already feel short.
A ten-day baseline
Egyptian historical travel reads more easily when built along the Nile.

The north has Cairo and Giza. Old Kingdom pyramids, the medieval Islamic city, the modern capital, and the present-day Grand Egyptian Museum. The south has Aswan. Granite, islands, Nubia, Philae, the High Dam, the doorway to Lake Nasser. Between them sits Luxor. Ancient Thebes, with the densest survival of New Kingdom temples and royal tombs.
In ten days, these three are the columns.

For transfers, domestic flights are practical. Driving Cairo to Aswan or back from Luxor to Cairo entirely by road eats time and stamina. The sleeper train is an option; on a first trip prioritising content, the flight is more stable.
Two orders.
One starts in Cairo, flies south, runs Aswan to Luxor, and returns to Cairo. International connections fit best; this is the most common shape.
The other starts in Aswan. Cairo's intensity sits at the back; you enter the trip from the gentler south. A beautiful sequence when international schedules allow.
This model is written for the Cairo-start shape.
Day 1: arrive in Cairo
Keep the first day light.

Cairo is large and traffic is heavy; a first arrival wants time. Move from the airport to the hotel, sort exchange and SIM, set the next day's flow. A light dinner in Zamalek or along the Nile is enough.
Choose the hotel by how you'll use the first two days. To go to
the Giza plateau
early next morning, a Giza-side hotel is practical. To also see the city's museums and old quarters, Zamalek, Garden City, or the Nile side moves easier.
With ten days, you can afford to not push day one. Not creating fatigue on the first night matters more than expected.
Day 2: the Giza plateau and the GEM
Morning at the plateau.

Enter as early as possible. To see Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure, the Sphinx, the valley temple, and the topography, the morning light and cool are best. Entering the Great Pyramid needs a separate ticket. Narrow, hot, and tiring — not required.

Afternoon at the Grand Egyptian Museum. Near the plateau, the GEM shows the Tutankhamun collection, Khufu's boat, and large ancient Egyptian display across the pyramid age into the New Kingdom and beyond.

The combination is natural; not a light day. Pairing pyramids and GEM means lunch and breaks must be real. People who don't want to skim the museum can split the GEM to another day. Ten days allows it.
Day 3: read Cairo
Day three goes to Cairo itself.
Two options. One: a day with NMEC,
Coptic Cairo
, and Islamic Cairo.
The National Museum
of Egyptian Civilization shows the royal mummies and the flow of civilisation; Coptic Cairo walks the church group and old city layer; the afternoon runs the Sultan Hasan Mosque or
Khan el-Khalili
area.

The other: Saqqara, Memphis, and Dahshur. For pyramid history in depth. Djoser's step pyramid, the Bent Pyramid, the Red Pyramid show that Giza is not a sudden miracle but the result of long architectural experiment over generations.
For a first traveller, both have value. For architectural flow, Saqqara and Dahshur. For the depth of Cairo as a city, NMEC and the old quarters. In ten days, you pick one here.
What you choose shapes the character of the trip.
Day 4: to Aswan
Morning flight to Aswan.
Aswan can feel like another country from Cairo. The Nile is wide, islands are many, the light is soft. Granite rocks, sandy banks, and Nubian colour make a southern air different even from Luxor.

Afternoon, Philae. Dedicated to Isis and now on Agilkia Island. The original Philae Island faced danger from changing water levels; the temple was moved through international rescue. Including the boat crossing, among the most beautiful visits in Aswan.
With time, add
the Unfinished Obelisk
or the High Dam. Don't pack on a transfer day. Keep evening time for the Corniche or a felucca, watching the river.
Day 5: Abu Simbel
Early-morning start to Abu Simbel.
South of Aswan, near Lake Nasser. By road about three hours each way; depending on arrangement, an early-morning departure. There are seasons and flights that fit; confirm operating status.

The Great Temple of Ramses II and the smaller temple of Nefertari are among Egypt's most powerful monuments. Colossal figures cut into the sandstone cliff, interior columns, victory scenes, the solar alignment. And the twentieth-century relocation during the dam project. Ancient and modern engineering layered at the same place.
A day trip return tires you in the afternoon. Don't add a large Aswan plan for that day. A quiet dinner and preparation for the next day's Nile transfer is the realistic move.

There is also the option of staying overnight at Abu Simbel and seeing the temples both afternoon and morning. On a first ten-day trip, that's a little specialist. For strong interest, a good choice; for the standard model, the day trip is enough.
Day 6: deepen Aswan
Easily cut on a seven-day trip; on ten, this day stays.
The Nubian Museum

is among the most important places in Aswan. It covers Nubian history and culture from prehistory to the modern era and shows the relocation issues caused by the High Dam. After Philae and Abu Simbel, visiting here makes the human displacement behind the relocated temples visible.
Elephantine Island
is another good choice. The ancient town, the Temple of Khnum, the Nilometer — measuring Nile water levels mattered for the state and agriculture.
Afternoon for a Nubian village or a felucca. Nubian villages are places where people live, not backdrops for photos. Treat the visit as a small encounter with present Nubian culture.
This day pulls the trip away from a chain of temples. The value of ten days sits in that margin.
Day 7: north to Luxor via
Kom Ombo
and Edfu
From Aswan to Luxor.

For a Nile cruise, the segment runs several days. To see Cairo, Aswan, and Luxor well in ten days, the cruise's nights can squeeze the schedule. Choose a short cruise or a private car that stops at Kom Ombo and Edfu on the way.

Kom Ombo is the double temple dedicated to Sobek and Haroeris. The left-and-right split structure reads clearly; the position right beside the Nile is striking. A small museum displaying crocodile mummies adds reality to the cult.

Edfu's Temple of Horus is famous for preservation. A Ptolemaic-period temple where the pylon, court, hypostyle hall, and sanctuary read very legibly. Among the clearest places to learn the "form" of an ancient Egyptian temple.
Arrive in Luxor in the evening or at night. Don't load on arrival. Luxor starts the next day.
Day 8: the Luxor west bank
The west bank is not a place to rush.

Morning at the Valley of the Kings. Ideally as early as possible. Beyond the standard ticket, Seti I, Ramses V and VI, Tutankhamun may need separate tickets. Choose by the day's open status and interest.

Quality over quantity. The wall paintings are not decoration. They are maps of the sun god's night journey, the dead's rebirth, kingship, and the underworld. A good Egyptologist guide changes the experience considerably.

After the Valley, the Hatshepsut mortuary temple. The three terraces set against the cliff carry an architectural force completely different from the underground tombs. With time and energy, consider Medinet Habu. Ramses III's mortuary temple is excellent for preservation, colour, relief, and the legibility of the space.
The Colossi of Memnon tend to be a short stop, not only a photo point. There once stood the enormous mortuary temple of Amenhotep III behind them. What you see is only the doorway to a lost scale.
The west bank is enough for one day. Adding Luxor Temple in the evening is possible; with fatigue, defer to the next day.
Day 9: Karnak and Luxor Temple
Day nine is the east bank.

Karnak is one of the places in Luxor most worth time. Not one temple — a religious city added to for centuries. The Great Temple of Amun, the Great Hypostyle Hall, the sacred lake, the obelisks, the surrounding smaller temples. On the surface you can run through fast; to see with meaning, give it half a day.
The Great Hypostyle Hall in particular cannot be photographed. Standing inside the stone forest of 134 columns, you feel in the body how New Kingdom power and religion came up as architecture.

Afternoon, rest a little. Evening at Luxor Temple. The temple sits in the centre of the town. Modern road, shops, the Nile, the lit columns close by — an intimacy different from Karnak. Visiting late afternoon into night, the feeling of a temple surviving inside the city becomes strong.
With time, the Luxor Museum is worth fitting in. Not large; the display is high-quality and quietly orders the context of the temples and royal tombs you've seen.
To give two days to Luxor in a ten-day trip is large. Compressing it into one thins the core of Egypt.
Day 10: back to Cairo
The last day flies back to Cairo for the flight.
With an evening international flight, you may get half a day in Cairo. Avoid big outings. Considering traffic, domestic-flight delays, and the airport transfer, give the last day margin.

With time, fit in something you didn't choose on day one — NMEC, Coptic Cairo, the Egyptian Museum, or hotel rest before the airport. With fatigue, don't force more sightseeing; the trip's impression ends better.
What matters on the last day of ten days is closing cleanly. In Egypt, leaving a little space at the end works better than cramming a final half-day.
With a cruise
You can include a Nile cruise in ten days.
The shape changes greatly with the number of cruise nights. A standard 3- or 4-night cruise links Aswan and Luxor (either direction) efficiently. Edfu and Kom Ombo fit naturally.
A dahabiya or a slower 7-night boat shifts the trip's centre of gravity onto the Nile. A beautiful choice; it cuts free time in Cairo and Luxor.
On a first ten days, two frames.
For efficiency, a short cruise or land transfer. You keep your own time in Aswan and Luxor.
For boat travel, a dahabiya or upper-end cruise at the centre. Be prepared to cut Saqqara, old Cairo, and additional Luxor sites.
Both are right. With a boat, the sailing date sets the whole itinerary. Better to design boat and domestic flights together than to lock in international flights and try to force a boat to match.
What to cut
Even in ten days, cuts are necessary.

Leave the Red Sea out on this trip. Hurghada, Sharm el-Sheikh, and Marsa Alam each have value; the sea does not bloom in a single night. Adding it wants at least two or three nights, which will thin Luxor or Aswan.

Alexandria is another candidate to leave out this time. A very interesting Mediterranean city; on a ten-day trip with serious Cairo, Aswan, and Luxor priority, it drops in rank. Fit it in on a second trip or one with longer Cairo time.
The White Desert and Siwa are lead destinations of different trips. Siwa especially is far and uses days just on transfer. Not an addition to a Nile-centred ten-day trip.
The thing not to cut is Luxor time. First travellers tend to finish Luxor in a day; that is a waste. With ten days, split west and east banks. That alone changes the quality.
When to use a guide
You don't need a guide every day.

At the Valley of the Kings, Karnak, Giza, and the GEM, a good guide's value is high. Wall paintings and temple structure read completely differently with explanation. In Luxor especially, a guide is not just an explainer — they judge which tombs are open that day, supplementary tickets, crowding, sun, and route.

In Cairo's old city and markets, a guide makes movement and bargaining easier. By contrast, late afternoons in Aswan or Nile-side walks can hold some free time. Filling everything with guiding turns the trip into a lecture.
A good ten days needs both the time of explanation and the time of looking without being explained to.
The value of ten days
Ten days makes Egypt look a little different.

In seven, the trip becomes "linking the representative places." In ten, you can leave margin at one or two. Go to the Nubian Museum in Aswan. Don't finish the Luxor west bank in a day. Don't rush the GEM. Include Saqqara and Dahshur, and understand Giza inside architectural history.
That margin changes the trip.
Egypt is not a country you understand by adding numbers. The fewer places you choose to see well, the more you see overall.
In ten days, you can draw one strong line.
Start in Cairo and Giza, see water and the south at Aswan, feel state monumentality at Abu Simbel, enter the density of temples and tombs at Luxor.
That is not all of Egypt.
As a first trip, it is a deep enough beginning.

deck: How to combine Cairo, Giza, Aswan, Abu Simbel, the Nile, and Luxor in ten days. An honest model itinerary for a first-time traveller.
